claims.claim: Moses brought Israel from the Red Sea into the wilderness of Shur; they went three days and found no water (15:22–23).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 15:22–23, read in full (`source-bible-gateway-kjv`).

claims.claim: At Marah the people murmured against Moses; Moses cried to the LORD, who showed him a tree; cast into the waters, they were made sweet (15:24–25a).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 15:24–25. The tree's species is unspecified in the text.

claims.claim: At Marah God "made for them a statute and an ordinance, and there he proved them", with the promise "I will put none of these diseases upon thee, which I have brought upon the Egyptians: for I am the LORD that healeth thee" (15:25b–26).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 15:25–26. First "statute and ordinance" language in Exodus.

claims.claim: At Elim were twelve fountains of water and threescore and ten palm trees, and they encamped there by the waters (15:27).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 15:27; confirmed by Num 33:9 (12 springs, 70 palms).

claims.claim: The congregation came to the wilderness of Sin on the fifteenth day of the second month after departing Egypt (16:1).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 16:1.

claims.claim: The whole congregation murmured against Moses and Aaron for want of food: "Would to God we had died... when we sat by the flesh pots, and when we did eat bread to the full!" (16:2–3).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 16:2–3.

claims.claim: The LORD promised: "I will rain bread from heaven for you... that I may prove them, whether they will walk in my law, or no" (16:4).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 16:4.

claims.claim: On the sixth day they shall gather twice as much as they gather daily (16:5).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 16:5.

claims.claim: Quail in the evening and bread in the morning; "then ye shall know that the LORD hath brought you out of the land of Egypt" (16:6–8, 12).

In the evening the quails came up and covered the camp; in the morning the dew lay round about, and when it went up there lay "a small round thing, as small as the hoar frost on the ground" (16:13–14).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 16:13–14; NETS 16:14 "fine like coriander, white like frost on the ground".

claims.claim: The people said "What is this?" (*man hu*); Moses said, "This is the bread which the LORD hath given you to eat" (16:15).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 16:15; BDB H4478 on the folk etymology (clm-wi-046).

claims.claim: An omer for every man, according to his eating; "he that gathered much had nothing over, and he that gathered little had no lack" (16:16–18).
"Let no man leave of it till the morning"; what was left bred worms and stank (16:19–20).
They gathered it morning by morning; "when the sun waxed hot, it melted" (16:21).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 16:21.

claims.claim: On the sixth day they gathered twice as much bread, two omers for one man; and all the rulers of the congregation came and told Moses (16:22).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 16:22.

claims.claim: "To morrow is the rest of the holy sabbath unto the LORD... bake that which ye will bake to day, and seethe that ye will seethe"; what was laid up for the morrow did not stink (16:23–24).
On the seventh day there was none in the field; some went out to gather and found none; the LORD rebuked them: "How long refuse ye to keep my commandments and my laws?" (16:25–28).
"See, for that the LORD hath given you the sabbath, therefore he giveth you on the sixth day the bread of two days" (16:29).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 16:29; NETS Greek reads "this day, the sabbaths" (clm-wi-083).

claims.claim: "So the people rested on the seventh day" (16:30).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 16:30.

claims.claim: The house of Israel called it Manna: "it was like coriander seed, white; and the taste of it was like wafers made with honey" (16:31).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 16:31; BDB H1407 (*gad*, coriander).

claims.claim: An omer of manna was laid up before the LORD, "to be kept for your generations"; Aaron "laid it up before the Testimony" (16:32–34).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 16:32–34; cf. Heb 9:4 (conn-wi-023).

claims.claim: "The children of Israel did eat manna forty years, until they came to a land inhabited... unto the borders of the land of Canaan" (16:35).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 16:35; cf. Josh 5:12 (conn-wi-026).

claims.claim: "Now an omer is the tenth part of an ephah" (16:36).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 16:36; BDB H6016 (clm-wi-047).

claims.claim: The congregation journeyed from the wilderness of Sin "after their journeys, according to the commandment of the LORD", and pitched in Rephidim, "where was no water for the people to drink" (17:1).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 17:1; K&D on "according to their journeys" (*lĕmasʿêhem*).

claims.claim: The people chode with Moses: "Give us water that we may drink... Wherefore is this that thou hast brought us up out of Egypt, to kill us and our children and our cattle with thirst?" (17:2–3).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 17:2–3.

claims.claim: Moses cried unto the LORD: "What shall I do unto this people? they be almost ready to stone me" (17:4).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 17:4.

claims.claim: The LORD said: take the rod "wherewith thou smotest the river", stand "upon the rock in Horeb", smite it, and water shall come out; Moses did so "in the sight of the elders of Israel" (17:5–6).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 17:5–6. The rock is located "in Horeb" by the text itself.

claims.claim: He called the place Massah and Meribah, "because of the chiding of the children of Israel, and because they tempted the LORD, saying, Is the LORD among us, or not?" (17:7).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 17:7.

claims.claim: "Then came Amalek, and fought with Israel in Rephidim" (17:8).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 17:8. No motive is given in Exodus.

claims.claim: Moses said to Joshua: "Choose us out men, and go out, fight with Amalek: to morrow I will stand on the top of the hill with the rod of God in mine hand" (17:9).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 17:9. First mention of Joshua son of Nun.

claims.claim: Joshua did as Moses had said and fought with Amalek; Moses, Aaron and Hur went up to the top of the hill (17:10).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 17:10.

claims.claim: When Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed; when he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed (17:11).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 17:11. The text states the correlation without explaining it.

claims.claim: Moses' hands were heavy; they took a stone and put it under him; Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands, one on one side and the other on the other, "until the going down of the sun" (17:12).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 17:12.

claims.claim: Joshua "discomfited Amalek and his people with the edge of the sword" (17:13).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 17:13.

claims.claim: "Write this for a memorial in a book, and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua: for I will utterly put out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven" (17:14).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 17:14. First command to write in the Pentateuch.

claims.claim: Moses built an altar and called it Jehovah-nissi; "the LORD hath sworn that the LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation" (17:15–16).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 17:15–16. The Hebrew of 17:16 is ambiguous (throne/banner — see §8.4).

claims.claim: Jethro, the priest of Midian, Moses' father in law, heard all God had done and brought Zipporah and the two sons — Gershom ("I have been a stranger in a strange land") and Eliezer ("The God of my father... delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh") — to Moses "where he encamped at the mount of God" (18:1–6).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 18:1–6. "The mount of God" before Sinai is the chronology problem (§8.3).

claims.claim: Moses went out to meet Jethro, did obeisance and kissed him, told him all the LORD had done; Jethro rejoiced and confessed, "Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods" (18:7–11).
Jethro took a burnt offering and sacrifices for God, and Aaron and all the elders of Israel came to eat bread with Moses' father in law before God (18:12).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 18:12.

claims.claim: On the morrow Moses sat to judge the people "from the morning unto the evening"; Jethro said, "The thing that thou doest is not good... Thou wilt surely wear away" (18:13–18).
Jethro's counsel, first part: "Be thou for the people to God-ward, that thou mayest bring the causes unto God: and thou shalt teach them ordinances and laws" (18:19–20).

Jethro's counsel, second part: "provide out of all the people able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, and rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens" (18:21).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 18:21.

claims.claim: "Let them judge the people at all seasons: and it shall be, that every great matter they shall bring unto thee, but every small matter they shall judge... If thou shalt do this thing, and God command thee so, then thou shalt be able to endure" (18:22–23).

Moses hearkened to his father in law and chose able men out of all Israel, making them heads — rulers of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens — who "judged the people at all seasons: the hard causes they brought unto Moses, but every small matter they judged themselves" (18:24–26).
"And Moses let his father in law depart; and he went his way into his own land" (18:27).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 18:27.

claims.claim: *Mān* (H4478): "What is it?" is a popular (folk) etymology for the name; BDB records the tamarisk exudate of west Sinai as the substance the Bedouin call manna.
claims.evidence: BDB H4478 via BibleHub, read directly (`source-bdb-lexicon`); Sarna agrees ("*man hu* is a folk explanation... The usual Hebrew would be *mah hu*").

claims.claim: *ʿŌmer* (H6016) is a dry measure, a tenth of an ephah; from the root *ʿamar*, "to press, squeeze, collect, and bind together" (a sheaf).
claims.evidence: BDB H6016 via BibleHub; Ex 16:36; Clarke Ex 16:16 ("about three quarts English").

claims.claim: *Mārâ* (H4785), "bitter": Marah's name encodes the bitterness of its water.
claims.evidence: Ex 15:23 (the text gives the explanation); BDB H4785 (not read directly — cited via the text and Josephus Ant. 3.1, "Mar = bitterness").

claims.claim: *Massâ* (H4532, "trial, proving") and *Mĕrîbâ* (H4809, "strife, contention"): the names at Rephidim encode the people's tempting and chiding.
claims.evidence: Ex 17:7 (the text gives the explanation); K&D Ex 17 on the names as a memorial "so the sin might never be forgotten".

claims.claim: *Śĕlāw* (H7958), "quail", occurs only four times in the Hebrew Bible (Ex 16:13; Num 11:31, 32; Ps 105:40).
claims.evidence: BibleHub lexicon / *Encyclopedia of the Bible* "Quail" (via Bible Gateway); Ex 16:13; Num 11:31–32; Ps 105:40.

claims.claim: *Šabbātôn* is an abstract noun denoting "rest"; *šabbāy* is the concrete "observer", from which it became the technical term for the seventh day.
claims.evidence: K&D Ex 16:22–26, read via truthaccordingtoscripture.com. Lexical analysis, not a textual statement.

claims.claim: Marah is most often identified with Ain Hawarah, a bitter spring about 50 miles south of Suez.
claims.evidence: JFB on Ex 15, read in full: Marah is "almost universally believed to be what is now called Howarah, in Wady Amarah, about thirty miles from the place where the Israelites landed on the eastern shore of the Red Sea." K&D on Ex 15, read in full: the well of Howra, 33 English miles from Ayun Musa, "both favour the identity of Howra and Marah"; "from the time of Burckhardt, who was the first to rediscover the well, Howra has been regarded as the Marah of the Israelites." The "about 50 miles south of Suez" figure is Hyatt's (1971, p. 172), as quoted in the station literature.

claims.claim: Elim is commonly identified with Wadi Gharandel, a well-watered wadi with palms.
claims.evidence: JFB on Ex 15, read in full: Elim is "supposed to be what is now called Wady-Ghurandel, the most extensive watercourse in the western desert — an oasis, adorned with a great variety of trees, among which the palm is still conspicuous." K&D on Ex 15, read in full: Elim "has been sought from olden time in the Wady Gharandel, about six miles south of Howra; inasmuch as this spot, with its plentiful supply of comparatively good water, and its luxuriance of palms, tamarisks, acacias, and tall grass... quite answers to Elim, with its twelve wells of water and seventy palm-trees."

claims.claim: The Hawarah→Gharandel distance (about two hours' walk) is too short for a day's march — a standing objection to pairing those two identifications.
claims.evidence: Bartlett 1879 — second-hand via summaries. An objection, not a refutation (no distances are given in the text).

claims.claim: Alternative Marah: Ayun Musa, the "Springs of Moses" on the east shore of the Gulf of Suez.
claims.evidence: Manning 1911; Robinson — second-hand via summaries. Underlying works not read directly.

claims.claim: Alternative Elim: Wadi Taiyibeh.
claims.evidence: Williams/Fosdick 1927, *National Geographic*, Dec 1927 — second-hand via summaries. Underlying work not read directly.

claims.claim: Rephidim is "now believed, on good grounds, to be Wady Feiran, which is exactly a day's march from Mount Sinai, and at the entrance of the Horeb district".
claims.evidence: JFB Ex 17:1, read via BibleHub (`source-jfb-commentary`). A reasoned identification, not a proof.

claims.claim: Rephidim is at Horeb itself, on the strength of "the rock in Horeb" (17:6) and "the mount of God" (18:5).
claims.evidence: K&D Ex 17 and Ex 18, read via truthaccordingtoscripture.com / Grace Notes PDF. Compatible with clm-wi-057 (Feiran is the entrance to the Horeb district).

claims.claim: Numbers 33:8–14 adds three stations Exodus omits — the Red Sea encampment (v. 10), Dophkah (v. 12), Alush (v. 13) — and names the first wilderness "Etham" (v. 8) where Exodus 15:22 says "Shur".
claims.evidence: KJV Num 33:8–14, read via BibleGateway/Bible.com (`source-bible-gateway-kjv`); Sarna on the condensed record (§5.1); K&D Ex 16:1.

claims.claim: Most stations of the itinerary cannot be located with certainty, and their modern identifications remain uncertain.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining Library, "Exodus" (overview article), read in full: "The narrative names its stations as though readers would know them, but most cannot be located with certainty today." BiblicalTraining Library, "Book of Numbers", read in full: "Many places in the journey cannot be identified with confidence. Most were temporary campsites in the desert rather than towns with lasting names, and the location of Mount Sinai itself is debated... Other reconstructions have been proposed, and certainty is not possible."

claims.claim: A real honeydew "manna" exists: scale insects (*Trabutina mannipara*, *Najacoccus serpentinus*) on the tamarisk excrete a sweet honey-like substance, appearing each June on the tender twigs for three to six weeks; the annual crop is small, usually only several kilograms.
claims.evidence: DeFoliart, "Southwest Asia" (Chapter 21, *Insects as Food*), read in full, reporting Bodenheimer (1929, 1947): "Bodenheimer (1947) argues that the manna of Biblical history (Exodus 16 and Numbers 11) was the excretion of two species of scale insects, Trabutina mannipara Ehrenberg and Najacoccus serpentinus Green"; "Here year after year in June appears a granular type of sweet manna from pinhead to pea size... for a period of three to six weeks"; "Usually the annual crop does not exceed several kilograms, but one steady man may collect over a kilogram a day at the peak of the season." K&D on Ex 16, read in full: the tamarisk manna exudes "in warm nights... in the form of small globules... honey-like taste," dropping "in consequence of the puncture of a small, yellow insect, called coccus maniparus."

claims.claim: The tamarisk exudate fails the biblical profile on every distinctive point: small quantities, not every year, cannot be baked (Num 11:8) or boiled (Ex 16:23), a medicine not food, well known to natives while Israel were strangers, no double-Friday / none-Sabbath / no-worms pattern.
claims.evidence: JFB Ex 16 and K&D Ex 16, read directly; Sarna (JPS, 1991) in the same terms. Consensus of the sources read.

claims.claim: The quail is the common quail (*Coturnix coturnix*), migrating in spring (Africa→Europe) and autumn across Sinai; exhausted birds fly low and are easily caught; Egyptian tomb paintings show quail-netting; the Ex 16 episode falls in spring (15th day of the 2nd month).
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining "Quail"; *Encyclopedia of the Bible* "Quail" (Bible Gateway); Herodotus 2.77 (Egyptians ate quail salted); mcgilvaryhouse. Natural-history consensus, second-hand in part.

claims.claim: Sarna's distinction: the quail "was a wholly natural phenomenon" except for its timing, while the manna "possesses a numinous quality" — no naturalistic explanation does justice to the manna tradition as presented.
claims.evidence: Sarna, JPS Torah Commentary: Exodus (1991), Ex 16 chapter, read in excerpt via pdfdrive PDF (`source-sarna-exodus`); quoted at length in the SD Jewish World article (pp. 75–76, 88). Modern scholarly judgment.

claims.claim: Internal date: the wilderness of Sin is reached exactly one month after the departure from Egypt (15th day of the 2nd month, 16:1).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 16:1; K&D Ex 16 (provisions "consumed in the 30 days that had elapsed").

claims.claim: Early date, c. 1446 BCE: the 480 years of 1 Kings 6:1, counted back from Solomon's fourth year, place the Exodus in the mid-15th century BCE (18th Dynasty).
claims.evidence: 1 Kings 6:1 (480-year notation) — cited via the BibleHub Q&A summary; the verse itself was not re-read in this session. A textual-chronological inference with no external corroboration.

claims.claim: Late date, c. 13th century BCE (Ramesside era): the store-city names and the Merneptah horizon favour a 13th-century Exodus, roughly the reign of Ramesses II (1279–1213 BCE).
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining Library, "Exodus" (overview article), read in full: "Other scholars place the exodus in the 13th century BC, during the long reign of Ramesses II (c. 1279–1213 BC). They begin from the store city of Rameses (Exod 1:11)... On the late view the exodus took place about 1270–1260 BC." The Merneptah Stele (c. 1208 BC) bounds it (clm-wi-068).

claims.claim: The Merneptah Stele (year 5 of Merneptah, c. 1208 BCE) is the earliest extrabiblical mention of Israel — "Israel is laid waste, his seed is not" — and fixes a terminus ante quem: Israel was a recognised people in Canaan by c. 1208 BCE. It says nothing about the Exodus itself.
claims.evidence: Merneptah Stele, verified via the Biblical Archaeology article, read in full (line 27; the people determinative; Petrie 1896; Spiegelberg; JE 31408); found 1896 by Petrie at Thebes; first read by Spiegelberg; Cairo JE 31408.

claims.claim: **Verdict:** no consensus date can be assigned to this category; the `date` field should be `unknown`.
claims.evidence: §7.1. A `proposed` value would pick a side in an unresolved dispute — FLAG F1, needs a material decision.

claims.claim: Josephus (Ant. 3.1): Marah is named from bitterness (*Mar*); the stick is split lengthways and the water "purged by drawing"; Elim's 70 palms are "ill-grown" and its 12 fountains "rather a few moist places than springs".
claims.evidence: Josephus, *Antiquities* 3.1, Whiston, read directly via Perseus/raptureready (`source-josephus-antiquities`). Reception — expansions with no basis in Exodus.

claims.claim: Josephus (Ant. 3.1): quails are "more plentiful in this Arabian Gulf than anywhere else"; manna is like honey, bdellium and coriander seed; *man* means "What is this?"; the supply lasts forty years; manna "even now... comes down in rain" in that place.
claims.evidence: Josephus, *Antiquities* 3.1, read directly. The present-tense rain claim is Josephus's own.

claims.claim: Josephus (Ant. 3.2): the Amalekites of Gobolitis and Petra, "the most warlike of the nations that lived thereabout", stir the neighbouring nations by embassy; Hur is "their sister Miriam's husband"; the altar is named "The Lord the Conqueror"; the Amalekites "should utterly be destroyed... because they fought against the Hebrews... in their distress also".
claims.evidence: Josephus, *Antiquities* 3.2, Whiston, read directly via Perseus. Reception.

claims.claim: Josephus (Ant. 3.3–4): Raguel (Jethro) came to Moses at Mount Sinai on hearing of his prosperity; he counselled rulers of thousands and hundreds, and Moses "complied in all things with his father-in-law's admonition".
claims.evidence: Josephus, *Antiquities* 3.3–4, read via Perseus search excerpts. Reception.

claims.claim: Philo (Mos. 1.206–208): the double portion proves the seventh day is the day on which creation was finished; the manna was ground, pounded and roasted "like honey cheesecake"; quails came in an uninterrupted evening cloud, flying near the ground.
claims.evidence: Philo, *Life of Moses* I §§206–208, Yonge, read directly (`source-philo-life-of-moses`).

claims.claim: Philo (Mos. 1.210–212): the rock — "whether it was that there was a spring previously concealed beneath it, or whether water was then for the first time conveyed into it by invisible channels" — Philo leaves the mechanism open; the rock supplied "for a long time an abundance of drink for so many myriads".
claims.evidence: Philo, *Life of Moses* I §§210–212, Yonge, read directly.

claims.claim: Philo (Mos. 1.214–219): the Amalekites are "the Phoenicians"; Moses' hands rose and sank "like the balances in a scale"; the altar he named "the refuge of God".
claims.evidence: Philo, *Life of Moses* I §§214–219, Yonge, read directly. "Phoenicians" is Philo's label, not the text's (rejected connection r4).

claims.claim: Jubilees 50: the wilderness of Sin is "the desert of Sin[ai], which is between Elim and Sinai"; the chronology runs 49 jubilees from Adam plus one week and two years (2410 AM), with forty years yet to come for learning the commandments; Sabbath law carries the death penalty.
claims.evidence: Jubilees 50 (Charles), read in full (`source-charles-jubilees`).

claims.claim: Augustine (CD 16.43): after the Red Sea, "for forty years the people of God went through the desert... when the tabernacle of testimony was dedicated... after the law had been very terribly given in the mount... on the fiftieth day after the passover was celebrated".
claims.evidence: Augustine, *City of God* XVI.43 (Dods), read via Logos snippets (`source-augustine-city-of-god`). Scope-append to the Genesis XVI union scope.

claims.claim: Calvin (Harmony, Ex 16): manna is "the bread of heaven" (Ps 78:24), Paul's "spiritual meat" (1 Cor 10:3), "a type of the flesh of Christ"; the daily portion proves obedience; the omer's equal distribution is Paul's pattern for almsgiving (2 Cor 8:14).
claims.evidence: Calvin, *Harmony of the Law*, Ex 16, read via sacred-texts.com / StudyLight excerpts (`source-calvin-harmony-of-the-law`).

claims.claim: Calvin, Clarke and K&D agree the Sabbath was hallowed before the promulgation of the Law: Calvin — "the seventh day was really hallowed before the promulgation of the Law, although it is questionable whether it had already been observed by the patriarchs"; Clarke — the Sabbath is "spoken of as being perfectly well known, from its having been generally observed"; K&D — "God bestowed His gift in such a manner, that the Sabbath was sanctified by it, and the way was thereby opened for its sanctification by the law".
claims.evidence: Calvin, *Harmony*, Ex 16:5; Clarke, Ex 16:23, 16:36; K&D, Ex 16:22–26 — all read via excerpts. See §8.2; FLAG F3.

claims.claim: JFB (Ex 18) and the majority of commentators: the Jethro episode is "inserted out of its chronological order" — it is set "at the mount of God" (18:5) though Israel did not reach Sinai until the third month (Ex 19:1–2; cf. Deut 1:6, 9–15).
claims.evidence: JFB Ex 18, read via BibleHub/bibleapps (`source-jfb-commentary`); Living Hope summary of Cambridge/JFB/Clarke/UCRT. See §8.3; FLAG F2.

claims.claim: Deuteronomy 1:6–17 retells the appointment of leaders as spoken at Horeb, which supports reading Exodus 18 topically rather than strictly chronologically.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 1:6–17 (retelling; cited via JFB Ex 18's cross-reference and the Living Hope summary — the Deuteronomy passage itself was not re-read in this session).

claims.claim: NETS (LXX) Exodus: the translator transliterates *mān* as "man" rather than translating "What is this?"; NETS 16:14 "fine like coriander, white like frost on the ground"; 16:31 "white like coriander seed"; at 16:29 the Greek reads "this day, the sabbaths" where the MT has "the sabbath".
claims.evidence: NETS Exodus (Perkins; Wevers Göttingen 1991), introduction + Ex 16 renderings read via archive.org djvu text (`source-nets-septuagint-exodus`). Translation facts.

claims.claim: Sarna's natural explanations: Marah's bitter water was filtered through porous wood (JPS Ex, pp. 82–83); the rock's water came from "water-bearing formations of soft porous limestone... A sharp blow to such rock may crack its crust and release a flow of groundwater" (p. 94).
claims.evidence: Sarna, JPS Torah Commentary: Exodus (1991) — quoted in secondary sources (LDS podcast notes, pp. 82–83; SD Jewish World, p. 94). Sarna's suggestions, not established mechanisms.

claims.claim: Amalek's motive, three readings: Josephus — fear of Israel's spreading renown, a defensive coalition; JFB — an old grudge, Amalek descended from Esau's grandson (Gen 36:12); K&D with Deut 25:18 — Amalek "fell on the rear" of the stragglers. No single motive is established.
claims.evidence: Josephus Ant. 3.2; JFB Ex 17; K&D Ex 17 — all read. Exodus itself gives no motive (clm-wi-029). See §8.4.

connections.note: The wilderness march departs from the far shore of the Sea — “So Moses brought Israel from the Red sea” (15:22).
The 15th day of the 2nd month (16:1) counts one month from the Passover departure (15th day of the 1st month).
The rod that struck the Nile (17:5, “wherewith thou smotest the river”) now smites the rock — the same rod links the plagues to the wilderness provision.
The Sabbath is given in the manna story (16:23–30) before the Decalogue (Ex 20:8–11).
“The mount of God” (18:5) anticipates Sinai; Jethro’s judges and the covenant law are retold together at Horeb (Deut 1:6–17).
The manna pot laid up “before the Testimony” (16:33–34) anticipates the ark and the Testimony of the tabernacle and the covenant.
The golden pot that had manna is placed in the ark (Heb 9:4) — the tabernacle’s furnishing completes the memorial of 16:32–34.
Jehovah-nissi (17:15) is the first altar built in the wilderness, the precursor of the altar of burnt offering (Ex 27:1–8).
The rulers of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens (18:21, 25) are the camp order under which the tabernacle is built (Ex 35–40).
The rulers of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens (18:21, 25) are the camp order under which the tabernacle is built (Ex 35–40).
Jethro, also called Raguel, is the father-in-law from Moses’ Midian exile (Ex 2:15–22; 3:1); Zipporah and the sons return to the story (18:2–4).
Amalek descends from Esau’s grandson (Gen 36:12) — the Amalek war is the Esau line’s hostility.
Midian is Abraham’s son by Keturah (Gen 25:2); Jethro the Midianite priest is of Abraham’s line.
The Sabbath’s seventh day is the day on which creation was finished (Gen 2:2–3; Philo, Mos. 1.207).
The manna as humbling and testing — “that he might make thee know that man doth not live by bread only”.
“Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way... thou shalt blot out the remembrance of Amalek” — the 17:14 command remembered.
The second quail and the second manna complaint; the people loathe the manna and are struck with plague.

The second striking of the rock at Meribah (Kadesh); Moses strikes twice and is told he shall not bring the congregation into the land. The two rock-strikings are distinct events — do not merge them.
The rock, the manna (“the bread of heaven”, “angels’ food”), the quail (“feathered fowls”) retold as a single history of provision and unbelief.
“The people asked, and he brought quails, and satisfied them with the bread of heaven. He opened the rock, and the waters gushed out.”
“Harden not your heart, as in the provocation, and as in the day of temptation in the wilderness” — Massah and Meribah as the standing warning.
“Did all eat the same spiritual meat; and did all drink the same spiritual drink: for they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ.”
“Our fathers did eat manna in the desert... I am the bread of life”; “Your fathers did eat manna in the wilderness, and are dead.”

The golden pot that had manna, in the ark — the memorial of 16:32–34 in its final location.
The Horeb retelling of the judges’ appointment.
The seventy elders — a second, distinct appointment of leaders; not the same as Jethro’s judges, and the two must not be conflated.
The manna ceased when Israel ate of the old corn of the land of Canaan — the forty years of 16:35 fulfilled.
Saul’s failure to blot out Amalek (Agag) — the 17:14 command left unfulfilled.
The retrospective — “Thou gavest them bread from heaven for their hunger, and broughtest forth water for them out of the rock”; forty years, “their clothes waxed not old”.
